Ceftriaxone may be used for empirical treatment where infection is thought to be caused by Streptococcus spp. and N. gonorrhoeae. Antibacterials 165 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) Empirical antibacterial treatment for infections caused by Gram-negative bacteria includes ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, or ciprofloxacin.4 Treatment of bone and joint infection is usually started intravenously; if high bone concentrations can be achieved with an appropriate oral antibacterial, pa- tients may be switched to oral therapy. Successful treat- ment of septic arthritis is generally achieved after 2 to 3 weeks of therapy, while osteomyelitis and prosthetic joint infections may need to be treated for weeks to months.5 A systematic review and meta-analysis6 of antibacterial treatment of bone and joint infections concluded that most studies were methodologically flawed and that there was little high-quality evidence regarding treatment. Ri- fampicin has also been used, sometimes with other drugs; in one study7 use of rifampicin with ciprofloxacin im- proved control of staphylococcal bone infections related to orthopaedic devices in comparison with ciprofloxacin alone. For reference to infection prophylaxis in orthopaedic pa- tients, see under Surgical Infection, below. Reactive arthritis is treated with anti-inflammatories; the role of antibacterials is less certain.8 Results in arthritis as- sociated with chlamydial infections have been more prom- ising than in that triggered by enteric infections.9 Long- term treatment with a tetracycline in addition to an NSAID has been reported to shorten the duration of reactive arthri- tis resulting from Chlamydia trachomatis infection.10 For mention of the use of tetracyclines, usually minocy- cline, in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, see under Musculoskeletal and Joint Disorders, p.350. 1.
